job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Yara Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Yara. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts around seven with a coffee and an AI assistant open on my laptop, because that's how I plan everything now. Mornings are lectures for my master's in data science at Lowmoor University. Afternoons I do freelance jobs, mostly fixing websites and booking forms for small shops, which brings in about 400 a month. Evenings I'm on a volunteer project, a stock-tracking app for the Eastgate food bank, and then I fall asleep in my hall room with the laptop on my chest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your first degree, and how did it end up?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science, a pass. I spent most of my final year building the food bank app instead of revising, and my exam marks dropped. I had no internship, and a lot of firms filter by grade. I owe about twenty-six thousand, and nobody in my family can help; my parents run a small corner shop and every pound goes back into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's less than people think, but it's already useful, which is what I see every day. I use AI for drafts, testing and debugging, and it's good, not magic. I'd tell friends that the hype is silly but the tools are worth learning anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes for me, and that's a worry because my problem is the grade. Firms near me still filter out a pass, and I've had maybe nine rejections from graduate schemes in a row. My freelance income is real but small, and one slow month and I can't cover my room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and try to lift my profile with a portfolio, not a grade. The food bank app is live and has real users, so I'd put it first on my CV. I'd keep freelancing and push the rate from 20 to 30 an hour. I'd also apply to startups, which don't care about the grade as much as bigger firms do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatient, more than scared. I know I can do the work, and I'm frustrated I can't get past the filter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push your rate. What would make a client pay more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proof, mostly. I've fixed a bakery's ordering system and a nail salon's booking page, and both owners will say it saved them hours. I'd ask each for a short written reference and use those to justify 30. Small business owners pay for someone who answers messages at ten at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a slow month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip meals and rely on the hall's cheap dinners, and I'd ask my mum to cover the phone bill, which she does without telling my dad. I hate that I'm taking money from the shop. That would be my low point.

I'd tell friends to build something real instead of waiting for a job.
think: My real problem is my **pass grade**, which filters me out of graduate schemes.
Freelance income is real but small, and one slow month would hurt my rent.

Raise my freelance rate from 20 to **30 an hour** with written references.
Apply to **startups** that care less about grades.
feel: **Impatient**: I know I can do the work and I'm stuck behind the filter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and that I'm already inside it. The coding, writing and testing tasks it takes over are exactly what a junior would've done. I'd say it publicly and I'd say unions and regulators have to step in before firms use it to cut every starter job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a double hit for me. Entry-level coding jobs get thinner, and the filter for a pass grade gets harder because firms can afford to be choosy. But I'm better with the tools than most graduates, so I might be the one a small team keeps. It's a coin toss, and I don't like coin tosses with twenty-six thousand on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double down on what I can do: build tools with AI, ship them fast and sell them to small firms who can't hire a developer. I'd put time into one niche, probably small food and retail businesses, since I already know their problems. I'd also ask the food bank to let me write a case study so I have evidence. And I'd start a small tech-workers group at the university to push for fair hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and scared in about equal parts. It feels like the ground is moving, but I'd rather learn to surf than stand on the beach and complain about the wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather learn to surf. What happens if the wave isn't big enough for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go back to the basics: stack shelves, stay in the shop with my parents, and keep freelancing. I'd never call that defeat, but I'd be angry, and I'd direct it at the firms that cut starter roles for profit. I'd rather help change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My coursemate Dev, who is great at maths but never touches the tools. He thinks they're cheating. In a world where firms expect the tools, someone like him gets left behind, and I'd feel awful watching.

steps.text: Build and sell a booking and stock tool to small food and retail shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, wow. I'd say we need rules and a safety net now: a public jobs plan, retraining and some form of basic income. Honestly I'd start a petition on campus the first week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's chilling. I'm good with the tools, but if AI can do almost any thinking work, then a freelancer in code is the first thing that goes, not the last. I'd have debt, no real savings and a degree whose entry jobs vanish. My parents' shop would be the only thing left that's tangible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the master's if a job came up. I'd double my freelance hours and try to turn the food bank app into a small paid service for other charities. I'd also help my parents with the shop's ordering, because it's a real business with real customers, and robots for hands-on tasks take until around 2031. I'd also join whatever group pushes for rules, because I can't solve this alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy. I'd be excited about the technology and furious about the timing at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shop is the only tangible thing. What would you actually do there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the ordering and stock system with AI, then cover a till shift or two. My dad says the shop barely makes a profit, but I'd be around people and I'd have a roof. It isn't a career, but it's something to hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave the master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone offered a job, yes, no hesitation. The course is about the world as it was a year ago. I'd rather be paid and learning on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is the version where you can do something useful. I'd say we should start retraining schemes, tax the firms making the savings and teach every student to use the tools now. I'd say it on campus and in my freelance chats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious, not alarmed. If I land a first job in the next year or two, I'd get a few years of real work before 2031. By then I'd be 29, with a proper portfolio and maybe a small business. The scary bit is that I might not get that first job, and the filter is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep freelancing, and apply for roles where AI skills are the point: data engineering, automation, anything that wires systems together. I'd save 120 a month toward the loan. I'd also try to build a product people pay for, because owning something beats begging to be hired. I'd join the tech-workers group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the two-year one. I'd feel a mix of focus and impatience, the way you feel before a big exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said owning something beats begging to be hired. Where would the first customers come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The food bank has a network of charities and they all struggle with stock and volunteers. If my tool saves them an hour a day, then I'd charge 40 a month each. Twenty charities is 800 a month, enough to live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who thinks the tools are cheating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a plumber with a better wrench isn't cheating, but your boss will assume you have the wrench, so it isn't optional. Then I'd show them one thing, not twelve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a gift. I'd say schools and universities should rebuild teaching around working with AI, and that every graduate should have a guarantee of a trainee place. I'd say it, but I'd also be busy building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm only uneasy, not worried for my own livelihood. By 2036 I'd be 34, I could have a small company, savings and experience across two cycles of technology. The unease is about my friends who don't adapt as easily, and my parents' shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take whatever first job gets me paid, and keep building the charity tool on the side. I'd save for a deposit and help my parents move the shop's orders online. I'd also study something new every year, maybe robotics or energy systems, because AGI isn't going to be the end of learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. I'd feel like I'm playing a long game for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said unease about your friends. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run free evening sessions at the library for people who think the tools are too hard. I wouldn't make a business of it, I'd just do it. People helped me when I was lost and I owe that back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good day look like in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mornings at my own desk, a couple of customers who pay on time, and a call with my mum about whether the shop sold out of oat milk. That's all I want.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because it leaves no time to learn or build. What would help is rules, a real public jobs plan, and trainee places for graduates, so that being good with the tools isn't the only thing between you and rent. And it would help if firms stopped filtering out everyone with a pass grade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd want people to know that being good with AI doesn't make you safe. It makes you faster, but you still need someone to give you the first job. I'm not scared of the machines. I'm scared of the people who decide who gets a chance.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the machines. I'm scared of the people who decide who gets a chance.
portrait: Yara is a 24-year-old computer science graduate with a **pass**, now doing a master's in data science.
She uses AI every day, freelances for small shops and built a **stock app** for a local food bank.
Her debt is about twenty-six thousand, and her parents' **corner shop** can't help.
She leans progressive: rules, unions and public support, and she blames firms and **grade filters**.
Her moods run from anxious to alarmed in the fast scenarios and **uneasy** when she has ten years to build.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because there'd be no time to learn or build.
whatWouldHelp: Rules, a **public jobs plan** and trainee places for graduates.
Firms that stop filtering out every **pass grade**.
